51633: Job shows Satan as a power nearly equal to God, who can do whatever he wants to believers, or alternatively, it shows God making a bet at a human's expense.
51634: In Job, 'the satan' is one of the heavenly beings presenting themselves before God, acting as an accuser. He can act only within limits God sets (Job 1:12, Job 2:6). The scene shows that human suffering is part of a larger story that the sufferer cannot see, not that God plays games. The book never lets Job learn about the scene, which is part of its point.
51635: Traditional readers see continuity with the later, fully developed Satan of the New Testament (Rev 12:9-10 calls him the accuser), and warfare theologians stress that real hostile powers exist. Both agree that Job places all such powers under God's ultimate authority.
51636: Overrating the satan leads to dualism and fear; reading the prologue as a cruel bet can make God seem a gambler. The text's restraint keeps the focus on whether faith can be free and on God's final authority.
51638: Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, much Catholic and Protestant tradition, C. S. Lewis
51639: God created everything good. Evil is not a substance but a privation, a lack or twisting of good. It entered through the free rebellion of angels and humans, and nature's disorder followed. God permits evil because he can bring greater good from it, supremely in Christ.
51640: Keeps God wholly good and evil wholly alien; takes human responsibility seriously; has deep roots in Scripture and tradition; explains why evil is parasitic on good.
51641: Struggles to explain how good creatures first chose evil, and how suffering among animals for millions of years can follow human sin. Critics say 'privation' does not capture how active and powerful evil feels.
51643: Humans were made immature and at an 'epistemic distance' from God in a demanding world, so that they could freely grow into mature children of God. Pain and danger make courage, compassion, patience and trust possible.
51644: Explains why the world is hard rather than a paradise; fits biblical themes of testing and growth (Jas 1:2-4, Rom 5:3-5); looks forward rather than backward.
51645: Much suffering crushes rather than builds character; infants and animals suffer without growing. Hick's dependence on growth after death and universal salvation is disputed. It can make God seem to use people as means.
51647: Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne, William Hasker, many evangelical philosophers
51648: A world with creatures who are significantly free is more valuable than a world of automatons, and genuine freedom includes the possibility of evil. It is possible that God could not create a world of free beings who never did wrong. This answers the logical problem and explains much moral evil.
51649: Widely accepted as defeating the strict logical problem; fits the biblical call to choose (Deut 30:19); keeps evil as the creature's responsibility.
51650: Does not easily explain natural evil without appeal to fallen spirits. Critics ask why God does not intervene more often, and how this fits with heaven, where the redeemed are free yet do not sin. Reformed critics say it relies on a libertarian view of freedom the Bible does not teach.
51651: John Calvin, Jonathan Edwards, Westminster Confession, D. A. Carson, John Piper, Paul Helm
51652: God ordains all that comes to pass, including evil acts, without being the author of sin, and humans are fully responsible (compatibilism). Every evil serves God's wise and good purpose, as at the cross (Acts 4:27-28) and in Joseph's story (Gen 50:20).
51653: Takes the Bible's strong providence texts at face value; offers deep assurance that no suffering is meaningless; honours God's glory and freedom.
51654: Many find it hard to see how God is not responsible for evil he decrees. It can sound cold to victims of abuse. Critics say it struggles with texts showing God's grief and opposition to evil.
51655: Many early church fathers, Gustaf Aulén (Christus Victor), Greg Boyd ('trinitarian warfare' model), many Pentecostal and majority-world Christians
51656: The world is a war zone. Rebellious spiritual powers, freely created by God, oppress creation and humanity. Much evil is not God's will but the enemy's work. Jesus' healings and exorcisms are acts of war, and the cross is the decisive victory, to be completed at his return.
51657: Matches Jesus' ministry and the New Testament's language of powers; lets believers call particular evils 'not God's will'; makes sense to many cultures that experience spiritual oppression.
51658: Difficult to verify; can make Satan seem too powerful or become an excuse for avoiding human responsibility. Reformed critics say it weakens God's sovereignty; scientists question it as an explanation of natural evil.
51659: Stephen Wykstra, Michael Bergmann, Daniel Howard-Snyder, many Christian philosophers
51660: Given the vast difference between God's knowledge and ours, we should not expect to see God's reasons for allowing many evils. So the fact that some evils look pointless is weak evidence that they are pointless.
51661: Modest and difficult to refute; matches God's answer to Job (Job 38-41) and Isa 55:8-9; can be combined with other views.
51662: Critics say it undermines moral judgement and the reliability of God's promises, and offers little comfort. Some say it would also stop us from inferring God's goodness from the world.
51663: Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, William Hasker, David Basinger, Greg Boyd
51664: God knows all that can be known, but future free choices are not yet settled facts. God takes risks, responds to prayer and can be grieved. Specific evils are not planned and some are pointless, though God works to redeem them.
51665: Takes seriously texts where God changes his mind or is surprised (Gen 6:6, Jer 3:7); frees God from responsibility for specific horrors; supports a relational view of prayer.
51666: Most traditions see it as denying God's full foreknowledge, which Scripture affirms in prophecy (Isa 46:9-10). Critics ask whether God's final victory is secure, and why God, if he can intervene, does not do so more often.
51667: Alfred North Whitehead, Charles Hartshorne, David Ray Griffin, John Cobb; related: Thomas Jay Oord
51668: God's power is persuasive, not coercive. Every creature has some self-determination. God offers each moment its best possibility and suffers with the world, but cannot unilaterally prevent evil.
51669: Removes the question 'why did God not stop it?'; presents God as the fellow-sufferer; fits a scientific picture of an evolving world.
51670: Gives up creation out of nothing and God's power to guarantee the final defeat of evil. Most Christians and Jews judge that it no longer describes the God of the Bible, who raised Jesus from the dead.
51672: Martin Luther, Jürgen Moltmann, Kazoh Kitamori, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, many liberation theologians
51673: God does not answer suffering from outside but enters it in the crucified Christ. God is known in weakness and godforsakenness. The cross shows God's solidarity with every victim, and the resurrection is God's promise that suffering will not have the last word.
51674: Centres on Jesus; offers deep comfort to victims; refuses easy explanations; joins theodicy to discipleship and solidarity with the oppressed.
51675: Classical theologians worry that some versions make God dependent on the world's suffering. Others note it says how God responds to evil but not why God permits it.
51677: The biblical lament tradition; Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev; Elie Wiesel; Emil Fackenheim; Eliezer Berkovits; Irving Greenberg; Hans Jonas; Harold Kushner
51678: A range of responses rooted in covenant: arguing with God on the basis of his own justice, refusing to let suffering destroy Jewish life and hope, speaking of God hiding his face, and in some cases rethinking God's power. Protest is treated as a form of faithfulness.
51679: Deeply biblical (Abraham, Moses, Job, the Psalms); refuses to explain away horror; keeps faith and honesty together; shaped by the most terrible evidence.
51680: Some forms (Rubenstein, Jonas, Kushner) give up the traditional God, which most Jews and Christians reject. Others leave the question unanswered, which some find unsatisfying, though its defenders see that as honesty.
